## Abstract {.unnumbered}

After the M7.5 earthquake that struck coastal Venezuela on 24 June 2026, at least eight
organisations released satellite-derived building-damage products. We evaluated the six that
published an analysed extent, scoring them not against a single expert reference but against
three with complementary blind spots: expert damage points from Copernicus EMS, crowd review of
AI-flagged locations, and 415 field reports. This lets the references check each other, and the
expert reference did not pass: it captured 94% of field-reported destroyed buildings but only
49% of those reported as significantly damaged. Every precision measured against it is
therefore a floor: Microsoft's rises from 0.08 to roughly 0.24 once crowd-confirmed damage is
counted.

At building level, every product performed poorly. As delivered, precision ranged from 0.01 to
0.08 (recall 0.31–0.69); even in the one damage-dense area where all six score best (the
Caraballeda AOI, which holds 96% of the reference) it reached only 0.04–0.09. None separated
itself from a deliberately simple benchmark that uses no satellite imagery at all: a model
built on coastline distance, building density and shaking intensity, fitted with hindsight to
this event's own damage map. That benchmark matched or beat three of the six there, and four
of the six across their full delivered footprints. At neighbourhood scale the products are usable:
they ranked sectors by damage burden reliably. But the same benchmark ranked those
sectors about as well, so this is where the products work rather than where they add.

The rest of their value lies in their disagreement. How many products must agree before a
building is flagged works as a dial a responder can set, from flagging every building any
product marked (97% of known damage, but 26 visits per damaged building found) to flagging
only unanimous buildings (93% of flags correct, 18% of the damage). Counting agreement
between methodologically independent products roughly doubles the accuracy of any single
product and requires no weights, no training data and no reference, which makes it the
only method we tested that is both effective and computable during a response; a
statistically fitted combination scores 18% higher, but fitting it requires the damage map
responders are still waiting for.

These findings come from one event and should be read as a case study and a reusable
evaluation method, not as general laws.

## Introduction

In the first days after a major earthquake, responders need to know where the damage is
and how bad it is, before ground access is possible. Satellite-derived damage products
fill this window, and their supply has grown quickly. The 2026 Venezuela earthquake drew
products from a variety of organisations: the EU's rapid-mapping service (Copernicus
EMS), a technology company (Microsoft AI for Good), universities (Oregon State
University, working with NASA; the University of Houston), an NGO (IMPACT Initiatives),
UN bodies (the UNEP/OCHA Joint Environment Unit; the World Food Programme, working with
the LIST and CERN research institutes), and volunteer AI platforms (HOT fAIr, DISHA).
These products disagree with each other, sometimes dramatically. A coordinator receiving
several of them in the same week has no established way to decide which to trust, for
what purpose, and at what spatial scale.

We evaluated the six products that published an analysed extent, scoring them against
three references rather than one: expert damage points (Copernicus EMS), a crowd review
of AI-flagged locations (MapSwipe), and reports from field teams on the ground (ChatMap).
Their blind spots differ (the crowd saw only flagged places, so it can refute false
alarms but never reveal a miss; the field reports are the reverse), so each reference is
used only for the question it can answer, and the three check each other. That checking
mattered: the expert reference turned out to miss half of the lesser damage the field
teams reported, so precision measured against it alone is a floor, not an estimate.

The paper is organised around three questions a coordinator would actually ask. Can a
responder act on a single flagged building? Do the products at least rank neighbourhoods
well enough to triage? And what is the sensible way to use them in the next event? Each
results section answers one piece, states how the answer was measured in a few
sentences, and points to the Appendix for the full method. Everything here comes from
one event in one coastal, dense-urban geography: the method transfers, and the specific
numbers should be treated as hypotheses until they are replicated.

## The event, the products, and the references

An M7.5 earthquake, preceded about 40 seconds earlier by an M7.2, struck near Yumare on
the Venezuelan coast at 22:05 UTC on 24 June 2026. Severe damage was concentrated along
the La Guaira coastal strip, in western Caracas, and in several inland towns. Copernicus
EMS rapid mapping was activated the same night (EMSR884).

We evaluate the six products that published a defined or defensible analysed extent, the
area the product actually examined (@tbl-products): without one, "no flag" cannot be
distinguished from "never looked", so neither misses nor false alarms can be counted
fairly. Two further AI products (HOT fAIr and DISHA) published no extent and appear in
the availability inventory only.

| Product | Provider | Sensing basis | Analysed buildings | Damage flags* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft AI4G | Microsoft | very-high-res optical + AI classifier | 72,162 (own footprints) | 8,410 |
| IMPACT v2 | IMPACT Initiatives | Sentinel-1 radar coherence change | swath (~372 km²) | 22,954 |
| OSU | Oregon State Univ. / NASA | Sentinel-1 radar coherence change | swath (~471 km²) | 31,259 |
| UH QuakeDamage | Univ. of Houston | very-high-res optical (Vantor imagery, author-confirmed) + AI classifier grading every footprint | 447,263 incl. intact | ~91k dmg/destroyed |
| LIST | WFP / LIST / CERN | AI change detection on before/after radar imagery (provider-stated) | 163,225 | 15,904 in core region |
| UNEP debris | UNEP/OCHA JEU | radar-derived debris mass per footprint | no extent (assumption, see Appendix) | 96,046 |

: Products evaluated. *Flag counts are as mapped onto the shared building-footprint base
used throughout this paper; totals differ from providers' native counts because of
footprint-base differences. OSU figures refer to its v0 delivery, the version available
during the response; a revised v1 arrived after the study window (@sec-casestudy).
{#tbl-products}

The sensing bases fail in different ways, which matters when the products are combined:
radar coherence methods are structurally resistant to the vegetation-change false alarms
that can fool optical and radar-brightness methods (the Appendix's sensing primer
explains why, with an agricultural control comparison from this event). Analysed extents
span three orders of magnitude, from Microsoft's single coastal strip (210 km²) to
LIST's two full Sentinel scenes (~224,000 km²); the like-for-like comparisons live in
the ~61 km² core region where all published extents and the reference overlap
(@fig-extents). Delivery timing is part of the picture, though this paper does not yet
analyse it: @fig-timeline reconstructs availability from our own ingest dates (an upper
bound; provider release dates are still being confirmed). The whole set arrived within
about eight days of the mainshock, and several products were sequences rather than
single artefacts, so the version a responder acted on depended on when they looked.

![Who analysed where. Each product's analysed extent, the five expert-mapped CEMS AOIs
(dashed black), and, in red with the zoom frame below, the ~61 km² core region where the
head-to-head, ensemble and fusion analyses live. UH publishes no extent (its polygon is
derived from its own classified footprints); UNEP publishes none at all and is scored
under a stated coverage
assumption.](artefacts/RQ0-matching-basis/figs/fig_extents_map.png){#fig-extents}

![Product availability, measured from the M7.5 mainshock: preliminary, pending provider
confirmation. Circles mark a release or version; a filled star marks the final product
actually evaluated. Positions are our-integration dates (an upper bound on
availability), so true release is earlier. Red markers are dates still to

**The three references, and what each can see.** Copernicus EMS provides trained-analyst
damage points and is the primary reference: every headline precision and recall is
computed against it, under one matching rule (a building counts as damaged if a CEMS
point lies within 10 m; the Appendix gives the reasoning and sensitivity). MapSwipe is a
crowd campaign in which more than 400 volunteers reviewed ~50 m cells at locations AI
products had flagged: it can refute false alarms but can never reveal a miss, so it is
used to adjudicate disputed flags, never as ground truth. ChatMap is 415 building-level
damage reports from field teams, positives-only with no survey frame: it can reveal
misses but says nothing about false alarms (@fig-refarch). Because their blind spots do
not overlap, the three can be turned on each other, which is how the expert reference's
own bias was measured (@sec-floor). One rule governs every number in this paper:
**against an incomplete reference, measured precision is a floor and measured recall is
a ceiling.**

![The three reference datasets at a glance. Two are HOT-run and easily confused:
MapSwipe is remote volunteers voting on ~50 m cells, used to adjudicate false alarms;
ChatMap is field teams reporting building-level points from the ground, used to reveal
misses.](artefacts/RQ0-matching-basis/figs/reference_architecture.png){#fig-refarch}
